notes:
I've gathered notes on most of the passage, but there are gaps. **I found nothing on vv. 42–50 (except a note on v. 50 and one on v. 49), 52–54, or the Orthodox and prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace views.** Enduring Word's page cut off before v. 28, and my reads of Matthew Henry's full chapter and StudyLight's v. 52 page failed. Those verses still need research.

**v. 28 – "Blessed rather…"**
- *Traditional reading:* Barnes (listed as Presbyterian/Calvinist) says Jesus grants that being His mother was an honour, but the chief happiness, the highest honor, was to obey the word of God. Matthew Henry says Jesus does not deny what this woman said, nor refuse her respect to him and his mother. Instead He points her to something higher. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-28.html
- *Where Christians differ (Mary):*
  - Desiring God (Baptist site) says Jesus hold[s] us back from the kind of exaltation of Mary that we find in the Roman Catholic Church. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-to-become-the-mother-of-jesus
  - GotQuestions says the NASB's "on the contrary" suggests that their thinking about Mary's special status needed correction. https://www.gotquestions.org/virgin-Mary.html
  - Constable says the verse should warn us against venerating Mary too highly. Coffman (Restoration Movement) goes the other way: Jesus affirmed the praise of His mother but put spiritual kinship above earthly ties. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-28.html
- *Catholic reading:*
  - Catholic.com argues the Greek word *menoun* should mean "indeed, much more," not "on the contrary." On this view Jesus was heaping a twofold blessing upon the Blessed Mother. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/that-time-jesus-dissed-his-mom
  - A second Catholic.com piece says Mary is blessed not because of bloodline but because of faith (Luke 1:45). https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/jesus-puts-mary-in-her-place
  - Lapide (1614) says Christ does not deny that His mother is blessed, as Calvin would have us believe. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kja/luke/11-34.html

**vv. 29–30 – The sign of Jonah**
- *Traditional reading: the resurrection.*
  - Gill says that, like Jonah's three days in the fish, Jesus' three days in the grave and His rising would confirm He is the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/11-30.htm
  - John MacArthur (GTY) says the sign of Jonah then is the resurrection. He adds that the reference shows Jesus treating the Jonah story as true history. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/42-162/the-last-sign
  - Calvin: "they will hear the voice of a prophet risen from the dead." https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom32/calcom32.ii.xvii.html
- *A real debate: is the sign Jonah's preaching or his rescue from the fish?*
  - Ray Summers held that in Luke the sign is the preaching. Coffman (quoted on the same page) strongly rejects this, noting the sign was still future. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-30.html
  - Kelly says Jonah is a sign here not of death and resurrection, but by his preaching. Constable takes a middle line: Jonah's supernatural appearance and his preaching both signalled coming judgment. Same URL.
  - Utley (bible.org) says Luke stresses Nineveh's repentance at Jonah's preaching, while Matthew stresses the three days. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-11
- *Scholarly notes:*
  - The Expositor's Greek Testament points out the verb is "shall be," not "is." That hints at something still future, as if to say: wait and you will get your sign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/11-30.htm
  - Hastings' Dictionary calls the meaning somewhat obscure. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdn/n/nineveh-ninevites.html

**vv. 31–32 – Queen of the South, men of Nineveh**
- MacArthur stresses that these were Gentiles who will condemn privileged Israel at the judgment. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/42-162/the-last-sign
- Henry: Jesus' preaching far exceeds that of Jonas, yet no one turns from their evil way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-30.html

**v. 33 – The lamp on a stand**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the lamp as the sign: plain to see, yet still possible to miss. https://biblehub.com/luke/11-34.htm
- Desiring God reads the lamp as Jesus Himself, the light of the world, who must not be hidden or missed. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/be-careful-lest-the-light-in-you-be-darkness

**vv. 34–36 – The eye as the body's lamp**
- Gill: a "single" eye is the understanding opened by the Spirit to the gospel. An evil eye is a mind darkened toward gospel truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-34.html
- Henry: the eye is "evil" when judgment is bribed by pride, envy or love of the world. Same URL.
- Constable: the point is letting the light in by accepting Jesus' teaching; refusing it brings spiritual blindness. Same URL.
- Keener (quoted in the Light of Israel commentary) notes that a "single" eye normally meant a generous one. Same URL.
- The Bible Hub study notes link a "good eye" with generosity and an "evil eye" with greed or envy. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/11-34.htm
- Desiring God on v. 35: much that looks like light is not, so be careful what you find attractive. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/be-careful-lest-the-light-in-you-be-darkness

**v. 37** – Guzik notes that despite growing opposition, Jesus did not hate the religious leaders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/

**vv. 38–40 – Washing; outside and inside**
- Bible Hub notes the host expected the customary ritual washing (cf. Mark 7:3–4). The Pharisees' oral laws on washing were later written down in the Mishnah. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Luke_11_41_give_as_alms.htm
- Henry on v. 40: since God made both body and spirit, He expects us to care for both. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_011.cfm

**v. 41 – "Give as alms the things that are within"** (a hard verse)
- *What "within" means:*
  - The Cambridge Bible says the meaning is much disputed.
  - Pulpit, Meyer and Vincent read it as giving the food in the cups and dishes to the poor.
  - Others read it as "according to your ability."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/11-41.htm
- *Tradition notes:*
  - Calvin: it is not water, but liberality, that cleanses both men and food.
  - Clarke (Wesleyan) calls these verses very difficult.
  - Wesley: show your hearts are clean by doing the opposite of your greed.
  - Ellicott (Anglican): it sweeps away the whole fabric of the law of ceremonial purity.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-41.html
- *Does giving earn cleansing?*
  - Gill takes the clause as Jesus voicing the Pharisees' own view, who thought almsgiving justified them before God, rather than His real teaching. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/luke/11-41.html
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the verse is not about the merit of good works. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-41.html
  - Bible Hub notes that Tobit and Sirach (in the Catholic Old Testament) praise alms as atoning. It argues Jesus grounds the principle in a true heart, not in a work that earns merit. It also cites Chrysostom and Augustine. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Luke_11_41_give_as_alms.htm

**v. 42** – I found only the text, no commentary.

**v. 49** – Henry's comment on v. 49 is in the studylight v. 51 page but didn't come through in what I could read. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-51.html

**v. 50** – Gill says the blood was required of that generation at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/11-51.htm

**v. 51 – Abel to Zechariah**
- *Who is Zechariah?*
  - The Bible Hub notes identify him as the son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court (2 Chron 24:20–22). Because Chronicles comes last in the Hebrew Bible, Abel and Zechariah span all of Scripture. https://biblehub.com/luke/11-51.htm
  - The NET Bible notes say it is not clear which Zechariah is meant here, but probably the one in 2 Chronicles 24. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Luk+11%3A51&theme=wiki
  - Ellicott notes that Luke leaves out Matthew's puzzling "son of Barachias." https://biblehub.com/luke/11-51.htm
  - Coffman instead thinks Jesus meant a more recent, secret murder. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/luke/11-51.html
